terms.title: Terms
items: Sunrise/sunset: when the sun's upper edge touches the horizon, computed with the sun about 0.83° below it to account for refraction.
Solar noon: when the sun is due south and highest in the sky.
Civil twilight: while the sun is less than 6° below the horizon, bright enough to be outside without lights.
Golden hour: while the sun is less than 6° above the horizon, soft warm light for photos.

year.title: Through the year
items: Seoul's shortest day is the winter solstice (about Dec 22), about 9 h 34 min; the longest is the summer solstice (about Jun 21), about 14 h 46 min.
The latest sunrise comes in early January (about Jan 6 in Seoul, 7:47) and the earliest sunset in early December (about Dec 7, 17:14), because of the equation of time.
Places further east see the sun earlier: about 4 minutes per degree of longitude, so Busan is more than 10 minutes ahead of Seoul.

method.title: How it is calculated
items: An astronomical formula gives the sun's position. It matched all 7 of KASI's announced Jan 1, 2026 sunrise times to the minute.
Times are Korea Standard Time, rounded to the nearest minute.
Cities use coordinates near city hall; far east or west within a city can differ by about a minute.

items.a: The calculator opens on today for Seoul. Change the city to see that area right away.

items.q: When are the longest and shortest days?
items.a: The summer solstice (about Jun 21) is longest and the winter solstice (about Dec 22) shortest: about 14 h 46 min and 9 h 34 min in Seoul.

items.q: Why is the latest sunrise not on the solstice?
items.a: Because of the elliptical orbit and axial tilt, solar noon shifts a little each day, so the latest sunrise falls in early January and the earliest sunset in early December.
Just after sunrise and before sunset, while the sun is below 6° altitude: usually 30–60 minutes depending on the season.
It uses the same kind of calculation and usually matches within a minute; a value near a rounding boundary can differ by one minute.
